newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss researcher surprised by Nobel Medicine Prize.
newsitem.headline: Swiss researcher surprised by Nobel Medicine Prize.

text.p: Swiss scientist Rolf Zinkernagel, his small office jammed by visitors come to congratulate him, said he was surprised and pleased to be one of two winners of the 1996 Nobel Medicine Prize on Monday.
Zinkernagel, head of the experimental immunology institute at Zurich University, was granted the $1.12 million prize along with Australian-born Peter Doherty of the University of Tennessee, Memphis.

"I assume some things will change in my life now," Zinkernagel said between answering incessant telephone calls and shaking hands with colleagues in his two-by-three metre university office jammed with books and papers.
"But we know so little still that there is enough work to keep me busy for the coming years and decades," he added.
"I've had no time to think about what to do with the money," he said.

Swiss and foreign television teams appeared for interviews with Switzerland's 24th Nobel Prize winner, who had come to work in an everyday academic outfit of red striped shirt, brown corduroy trousers and worn leather shoes.
"Yes, yes, I'm very happy...I haven't had time yet to drink any champagne because the phone has been ringing constantly since I received the call from Stockholm," Zinkernagel told Reuters.
"Of course everybody who wins a Nobel prize is always surprised. But I really am surprised because a Nobel Medicine Prize was awarded for similar work in 1980," he added.
Zinkernagel has published about 200 papers on the medical battle against diseases caused by viruses.

Sweden's Karolinska Institute rewarded the two researchers for discoveries made while working together at a medical college in the Australian capital Canberra on how the human immune system recognises virus-infected cells.
Zinkernagel said the work done at the John Curtin School of Medical Research in Canberra from 1973 to 1975 had helped clarify how the body's network of immune cells identifies invading viruses.
Zinkernagel said he would celebrate with the staff of his 35-person institute -- but only after passing the news of his prize up to the head of the university.
"I don't think the chancellor knows yet," he said half an hour after being told of his achievement.
